title: The wretched man (Romans 7:14–25)
hook: the good I want, I don't do

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was baptizo, a burial and a rising. Your line was newness of life.

The alarm is set for six. The running shoes are by the door. The plan was made with a clear head and good intentions. Then six o'clock comes, and a hand reaches over and turns the alarm off. Or it's the sharp word someone swore they wouldn't say, out loud again. Wanting one thing and doing another is an old, ordinary human knot. The surprise is finding it in Paul's letter to Rome, right after his big picture of new life. He stops arguing, and writes in the first person about a war inside him.
screen: `THE ALARM, THE SHOES, THE SNOOZE.` → `WANTING ONE THING, DOING ANOTHER.` → `PAUL WRITES IN THE FIRST PERSON.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the King James Bible: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do." It doubles back on itself like the knot it describes. Paul says he agrees with God's law. He delights in it. He knows it's good. And still something in him pulls the other way, like a second law at war inside him. The knowing isn't the problem. The doing is. Then the paragraph breaks open into a cry: "O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death?" Wretched, talaiporos in Greek, means miserable, worn down by hardship. It isn't a pose; it's a groan. And notice the question. Not how do I fix myself, but who shall deliver me? He's looking outside himself. The answer comes in the very next breath: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord." Now a real puzzle Christians have argued over for a long time: who is this I? Some readers, including Augustine in his later years and Martin Luther, hear the Christian life: even the baptized still feel this war inside, every day. Others, among them early Greek teachers and scholars today, hear life under the law without the Spirit, the way things look before chapter eight. The text doesn't settle it for us. Either way, Paul writes in the present tense, and he doesn't flinch. He doesn't hide the struggle or scold it. He names it, and cries out for help.
screen: `THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.` · `TWO LAWS AT WAR INSIDE.` · `WHO SHALL DELIVER ME?` · `WHO IS THIS I?` · then, large: `O WRETCHED MAN THAT I AM!`

segments.voice: Name one small, real thing you keep doing that you don't want to do, and instead of the usual lecture, speak to yourself the way you'd speak to a friend who told you the same thing: tired, honest, still trying. Notice where the struggle sits in your body, and let your breath go there. If you pray, say Paul's own question, who shall deliver me, and just wait with it.
Talaiporos. Paul's Greek cry of wretchedness: worn down by the war between the good he wants and what he does.
Your line: who shall deliver me? It's a cry for help, not a lecture. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 7 when talking honestly about habits and temptation, in confession, in recovery groups and in spiritual direction, where the struggle is named without shame.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): new hook (alarm and snooze instead of late-night scrolling, which echoed day 318's practice); cut the superlatives 'one of the most driven people in history' and 'one of the most honest paragraphs'; cut 'everybody knows this feeling', 'you'll hear yourself' and 'almost every reader recognizes'; 'many early Greek teachers, and many scholars' became 'other readers, among them'; 'many centuries' became 'a long time'; trapdoor's 'among the most debated' softened.

Interpretive history: Augustine's later reading (e.g. against the Pelagians) and Luther's (simul iustus et peccator) take the 'I' as the Christian; many Greek Fathers and many modern scholars (following e.g. Kümmel, 1929) take it as life under the law. Confirm the summary 'many early Greek teachers'.
Changed 'sixteen centuries' to 'many centuries': the debate predates Augustine (Origen already discusses the speaker of Romans 7 in the 3rd century).
Softened 'the most honest paragraph in the whole letter' to 'one of the most honest paragraphs' (evaluative superlative).
Talaiporos glossed as worn down by hardship; confirm.
Practice invites saying Paul's own words ('who shall deliver me') if one prays; this is a scripture line, not a new prayer.
Restyled 2026-10-07 (job 2): voice tightened; content and sources unchanged.
